title: Textured buttercream with an icing spatula
subtitle: ripple, swipe, and wave patterns in the final coat of a frosted cake
excerpt: Textured buttercream is a finishing method where deliberate marks are pressed into the final coat of a frosted cake with an icing spatula. Work over a crumb coat that has chilled for at least 20 minutes. Warming the blade in hot water between strokes gives a cleaner mark with no tearing.
sourceNotes: Textured buttercream techniques documented in British and American cake-decorating manuals from the 1980s onward.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thin first layer of buttercream applied to a filled layer cake to trap loose crumbs before the final decorative coat.

content.text: Textured buttercream is a finishing method where an icing spatula leaves deliberate marks in the outer coat of a frosted cake. It works over a firm
that has chilled for at least 20 minutes. Warming the blade in hot water between each stroke gives a cleaner mark with no tearing or dragging.
Apply the outer coat about 5 mm thick. This gives enough depth to mark without cutting through to the crumb coat beneath.
Apply a 5 mm outer coat of buttercream over the chilled cake using the icing spatula. Smooth roughly with a scraper. A perfect surface is not needed at this stage.
Place the blade of the icing spatula in a jug of hot water for 10 seconds, then shake off excess water and wipe dry on a cloth.

Press the warmed blade flat against the side of the cake. Draw it across in one smooth horizontal stroke, lifting cleanly at the end. The hot blade releases from the buttercream and leaves a defined groove.
Re-warm the blade before each stroke. Start the next stroke 2 cm above the last and work up the cake. Stagger the spacing slightly for a wave effect rather than a grid.
Apply the outer coat and level it roughly. No extra chilling is needed between the coat and stippling.
Press the flat of the spatula against the buttercream, then pull it straight back off. Each press-and-pull leaves a rough peak. Work across the top and around the sides in overlapping presses.
Keep the spatula at room temperature for stipple. A warm blade gives a slightly smoother result, a cold blade gives more defined peaks.

attrs.problem: Marks dragging through to the crumb coat beneath
attrs.avoid: Avoid marking before the crumb coat has firmed. Soft buttercream beneath tears when pressure is applied from above.
attrs.fix: Chill the crumb-coated cake for a full 30 minutes before adding the outer coat. Then mark immediately while the outer coat is fresh.

attrs.problem: Swipe strokes not leaving a clean edge
attrs.avoid: Avoid a cold or dry blade; buttercream sticks to it and tears rather than releasing cleanly.
attrs.fix: Re-warm the blade in hot water before every stroke and dry it on a cloth each time. The warm blade slides through the buttercream and releases it cleanly as you lift off.

attrs.problem: Stipple peaks looking uneven and untidy
attrs.avoid: Avoid pressing and pulling at different angles; inconsistent direction creates a random rather than textured look.
attrs.fix: Keep the spatula perpendicular to the surface for each press-and-pull. Work from the top down the sides so the motion is consistent.
